Article Title: Search ops involving Indian Navy for 3 missing fishermen continue in Kerala: Official
Article Text:
INS Kalpeni sailed from Kochi on Saturday night to join the search operation and anchored one nautical mile off Neendakara on Sunday morning (Representative image)

NEW DELHI: A search operation involving the Indian Navy for three fishermen who went missing following separate boat mishaps off Kollam and Thiruvananthapuram coasts will continue on Monday, a defence spokesperson has said.The search operation for Gautam Krishna, John and Shijin -- who went missing in separate fishing boat mishaps at Neendakara (in Kollam), Vizhinjam and Muthalappozhi (in Thiruvananthapuram), respectively, on July 31 -- entered its 10th day on Sunday.On Sunday, Indian Navy divers joined the Coast Police, Coast Guard and Marine Enforcement Wing of the fisheries department to search for the three missing fishermen.INS Kalpeni sailed from Kochi on Saturday night to join the search operation and anchored one nautical mile off Neendakara on Sunday morning, the spokesperson said.The divers are using portable SONAR, which enhances their capability for underwater surveillance and diving operations, the spokesperson said. The Navy initially focused its search on Gautam Krishna, who went missing after his fishing boat capsized off the Neendakara coast. Later in the evening, INS Kalpeni moved to Muthalappozhi harbour to continue the search.
Article Summary: The search operation for Gautam Krishna, John and Shijin entered its 10th day on Sunday. Indian Navy divers joined the Coast Police, Coast Guard and Marine Enforcement Wing of the fisheries department to search for the three missing fishermen. The divers are using portable SONAR, which enhances their capability for underwater surveillance and diving operations.

Article Title: DGCA to conduct preliminary probe into Baramati aircraft runway excursion: Centre
Article Text:
No injuries as training aircraft veers off runway at Baramati airport

(With PTI inputs)

NEW DELHI: The ministry of civil aviation (MoCA) said on Sunday that a team from aviation regulator, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), is being sent to Maharashtra’s Baramati airfield, where a Cessna training aircraft was involved in a runway excursion earlier in the day.“The air safety team from the DGCA is going to the site to conduct a preliminary investigation and ascertain the circumstances and contributing factors leading to the incident,” the ministry statement read.MoCA further noted that the plane appeared to have sustained damage to its propeller, engine cowling and nose landing gear, while no fatalities or injuries were reported.“There were no injuries or fatalities reported. The aircraft has sustained prima facie damage to the propeller, engine cowling and nose landing gear. A detailed assessment of the damage will be carried out by the competent authorities,” the statement added.According to the ministry, the incident occurred around 12:25 pm when the Cessna C172, bearing registration VT-SEX and operated by flying training school Academy of Carver Aviation, veered off the runway at Baramati airfield.The aircraft was being operated for a Circuit and Landing Emergencies (CL Emergencies) training exercise.It was under the command of flight instructor Captain Chirag Shashikant Doifode, with trainee Abhijeet Jundre on board.The plane had taxied out at around 12:09 pm for the scheduled training exercise.“During the exercise, the aircraft entered the runway through Link Bravo and lined up at the threshold of runway 29, where a rejected take-off exercise practice was carried out.“Subsequently, the aircraft lined up at the threshold of runway 11 and another rejected take-off exercise was carried out,” the statement noted.During the exercise, the aircraft was unable to stop within the paved runway surface and subsequently veered off the extended paved surface beyond the threshold of runway 29 towards the right side, resulting in a runway excursion, according to the ministry.
Article Summary: A team from aviation regulator, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), is being sent to Maharashtra’s Baramati airfield. A Cessna training aircraft was involved in a runway excursion earlier in the day. The plane appeared to have sustained damage to its propeller, engine cowling and nose landing gear.

Article Title: Three incidents that shaped Kailash Satyarthi’s life and work
Article Text:
Shoeshine boy outside school

Friend who dropped out

Wasal Khan and Sabo

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Compassion and

AI ethics

In 1959, on his first day to school as a five-and-a-half-year-old in Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh, Kailash Satyarthi (he was Sharma then) spotted a shoeshine boy sitting quietly outside the gate. Curious and confused, he asked a teacher, “Why is a child sitting outside the school?” He was told that it is not uncommon for poor kids to work.Satyarthi was not satisfied. Every day, he would see the boy, roughly his own age, sit there with his father until one day he gathered courage and asked his father why his son was not at school. The man spoke with a deep hopelessness, recalls Satyarthi. He said, “Babu, school jaane ke liye aap log to hain. Hum to yehi kaam karne ke liye paida hote hain (There are people like you who go to school. We are born to do this kind of work). ”As a child, Satyarthi felt there was something wrong in this, but he couldn’t understand what. “I was taught that God has made us all equal. Why this inequality, I wondered,” he recalls.This encounter gave him a different perspective on life at a very early age.Satyarthi was just 11 when he found that his best friend and some other students had stopped attending classes in the new session.He was told that such dropouts happened because the poor could not afford even nominal fees and textbooks.Satyarthi wanted to do something. He got an idea and shared it with a friend. “My father had given me some money to buy sweets after I had cleared the examination. We went to a vegetable vendor, gave him the money and rented his pushcart,” he says.They went around the neighbourhood, urging people to donate the used books of their children, so that the needy could use them. “Within a few hours, the cart was full and we had to take a second turn. We collected 2,300 books that day,” he remembers.Soon, another idea — a permanent book bank for needy kids — was born, in which even headmasters and bookstore owners joined in. About 10,000 books were collected.Decades later, when Satyarthi went to Vidisha after winning the Nobel in 2014, he heard someone call out his name during an open-jeep parade. “The gentleman said, ‘I am a retired headmaster. I had almost quit my studies due to lack of money. But your book bank initiative allowed me to continue’,” Satyarthi recalls.It was quite a moment for both.At 27, Satyarthi had started a journal, ‘Sangharsh Jaari Rahega’, which spoke up for the marginalised and oppressed. The office was near Mandi House in central Delhi. One day, a sickly person in a lungi knocked on his door and passed out after a few words. He was carrying a copy of the magazine.When he regained consciousness, the man started whimpering, “Babuji, please save my daughter.” His name was Wasal Khan. Over the next few minutes, he poured out his life story. His wife and he were lured away from a village in Aligarh district, taken to Punjab’s Sirhind, where they had been enslaved in a brick kiln for 17 years. They worked without pay, given just food and used clothes to wear. “He said the owners were planning to sell Sabo, his 15-year-old daughter, to brothel agents from Delhi,” says Satyarthi. Wasal had escaped on the back of a truck and reached Chandigarh, where a magazine subscriber had given him an old copy and asked to go to Delhi for help.Satyarthi was faced with a tough choice: write an article or take action. He opted for the latter. He organised a truck and, on reaching the spot, he and his friends from Punjab — one of them had a camera — boldly told the lone gun-wielding chowkidar that they were journalists from Delhi. The watchman ran away. “We were about to leave with 36 men, women, and children when a police jeep arrived with the owners. They started slapping us and forcing the labourers to get down from the truck,” Satyarthi recalls. The truck driver had run away. Satyarthi and his friends too had to flee. “Our slippers were lost, our clothes torn.”Somehow they reached Chandigarh and then Delhi. “They had taken away the camera. But two reels, which vividly captured the labourers on camera, were with us. We had good evidence,” he says. Satyarthi approached Swami Agnivesh and, through him, renowned lawyer Gobinda Mukhoty, who filed a habeas corpus petition in Delhi high court. Since nobody knew the name of the brick kiln owners, a notice was sent to Punjab Police and the state.Eventually, Wasal Khan, Sabo and the rest were produced in court and freed.The children, who had grown up inside the brick kiln, had no idea of life outside. “As we walked from the high court towards our office, they were jumping like frogs released from a bucket, oblivious to the traffic. That day, I realised what true freedom really meant. I could feel God in their joy. We also knew this was the field where we have to work. Over the decades, our organisation, Bachpan Bachao Andolan, has rescued over 1,40,000 men, women and children,” he says.This is the age of AI and Satyarthi believes that technology should factor in compassion (karuna), which he defines as “a force born from feeling the suffering of others and drives us to take action.” Satyarthi feels that AI technology must be governed by a sense of responsibility during its designing, development and deployment. “AI should have a moral compass. It cannot just be profit-hungry,” he says.
Article Summary: Kailash Satyarthi was just 11 when he found that his best friend and some other students had stopped attending classes in the new session. He was told that such dropouts happened because the poor could not afford even nominal fees and textbooks. He wanted to do something. He got an idea and shared it with a friend.

Article Title: 'Yuvraj Singh asked me to stand on the chair': Mohammed Shami recalls first India dressing room experience

NEW DELHI: Mohammed Shami has opened up about his first experience inside the Indian dressing room and admitted that he was nervous after seeing several stars he had grown up watching. Shami had already made his ODI debut against Pakistan in Delhi on January 6, 2013. He made his Test debut later that year against the West Indies at Eden Gardens in Kolkata, from November 6 to 8. His T20I debut came against Pakistan in Mirpur on March 21, 2014.However, joining the Indian dressing room for the first time was a completely different experience for the fast bowler.Shami recalled attending his first team meeting and the moment Yuvraj Singh asked him to stand on a chair and speak to the team."The first time I joined the Indian team, I did not know how things were. There was a team meeting a day before the game. When I walked in through the door and looked around, there was not one name that had not come in my dream. I just sat quietly. Yuvraj Singh asked me to stand on the chair. What can you tell him? So I did that. He told me to give a speech. I had forgotten everything after seeing all the names. I could not say much. I just told my name and where I was from. I could not say more than that as I could not remember anything," Shami said.ID@undefinedCaption not available.ID@undefinedCaption not available.ID@undefinedCaption not available.The moment came at the beginning of a career that would see Shami become one of India's leading fast bowlers.Shami also spoke about the lighter side of the Indian dressing room and revealed the funniest player he played alongside.His pick was former India opener Shikhar Dhawan . The two spent several years together in the Indian team, with Dhawan playing 34 Tests, 167 ODIs and 68 T20Is before retiring from international and domestic cricket in 2024.Shami said Dhawan often knew how to lift the mood, even when India had suffered a defeat."Shikhar is very funny. He does those things. Say we lost a match, everyone comes and sits in the change room. Shikhar wants to do something different. He will just laugh very loudly. If I ask why are you laughing, he says because we lost. He does such things. Anytime, he will stand on the table and start dancing to Punjabi music. These things create that atmosphere in the dressing room. We also enjoy it because winning and losing keep happening.When you are playing the whole year, you will win and lose. All these things are there. But no one then goes into a very sad mood in the dressing room," the pacer said on cricketnextofficial.Shami has played 64 Tests for India and has taken 229 wickets, including six five-wicket hauls. He has also represented India in 108 ODIs, taking 206 wickets, including six five-wicket hauls.In T20Is, Shami has played 25 matches and picked up 27 wickets.His last appearance for India came against New Zealand in the Champions Trophy final in Dubai on March 9, 2025. India won the match by four wickets.
Article Summary: Mohammed Shami opens up about his first experience inside the Indian dressing room. The fast bowler said he was nervous after seeing stars he had grown up watching. Shami also revealed the funniest player he played with was former India opener Shikhar Dhawan.

Article Title: ‘Not taking up the position’: VVS Laxman reveals why he turned down India head coach job after Dravid
Article Text:
BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia, left, with BCCI Centre of Excellence (CoE) head VVS Laxman. (PTI Photo)

Laxman defends CoE amid injury concerns

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: VVS Laxman has revealed that he turned down the opportunity to succeed Rahul Dravid as India head coach in 2024, choosing instead to continue his work at the BCCI Centre of Excellence (CoE) and citing family considerations as one of the reasons behind his decision.The BCCI had approached Laxman after Dravid's successful stint ended with India's T20 World Cup triumph in 2024. However, the former India batter opted to extend his tenure at the then National Cricket Academy, which was subsequently rebranded as the CoE, for another two years until 2026.“Because (former BCCI secretary) Jay (Shah) and the BCCI gave me the freedom to execute my vision, and Devajit (Saikia, current BCCI secretary) continues to give me, I've extended (stint at CoE) for two years, and I committed to the BCCI that I'm not taking up the head coach position. You all know that I was approached back in 2024,” Laxman said at a presser at the CoE on Sunday.Laxman, who succeeded Dravid as the head of the NCA in 2021, said he wanted to establish the CoE's structure, processes and protocols before moving on.“I'll make sure that I establish the CoE, its structure, the processes and the protocols... before I move on, after the two years' stay,” he said.His comments come amid speculation that he could be considered for another prominent BCCI role, with his name being linked to the chief selector's position once Ajit Agarkar 's tenure ends in September. Laxman, however, did not indicate any decision on his future beyond his current CoE stint. Laxman also strongly defended the CoE's role amid concerns over the number of India players currently recovering from injuries , insisting that the facility should not be viewed merely as a rehabilitation centre.Jasprit Bumrah, Harshit Rana, Hardik Pandya, Washington Sundar and B Sai Sudharsan are among the players who have been recuperating at the facility.“CoE is not just a rehab centre, but there are bigger roles to play for it in helping cricketers achieve excellence,” Laxman said, stressing that injuries cannot always follow predetermined recovery timelines because “it is the human body” and “not a machine”.He said there was “seamless” communication between the CoE, selectors and team management, with players released only after meeting prescribed fitness benchmarks.Laxman also highlighted the development of young cricketers and his involvement in women's cricket as major achievements of his tenure.“Trophies are a by-product of what systems and processes you set,” he said, adding that the CoE's work was aimed at strengthening Indian cricket and helping players become the best they can be.
Article Summary: VVS Laxman reveals he turned down the opportunity to succeed Rahul Dravid as India head coach in 2024. The former India batter opted instead to continue his work at the BCCI Centre of Excellence (CoE) He cited family considerations as one of the reasons behind his decision. The CoE head also strongly defended the CoE's role amid concerns over the number of India players recovering from injuries.

Article Title: Tragic end for Jake Whisenant: Yosemite speed climbing star dies in Sierra Nevada accident
Article Text:
Jake Whisenant. Image via: @jake.doubleyew/ Instagram

Yosemite's El Capitan climber Jake Whisenant dies at 30 in a Sierra Nevada accident

Jake Whisenant dies at 30. Image via: @jake.doubleyew/ Instagram

Climbing community remembers Jake Whisenant

Jake Whisenant's record-setting climbs on El Capitan

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Jake Whisenant, the Yosemite speed climber who holds the record time up El Capitan's Lurking Fear route, has died in an accident in the Sierra Nevada. He was 30.The Tulare County Sheriff's Office Coroner recorded his date of death as August 3, according to multiple reports. Officials have not released details about the circumstances of the accident, and his death has drawn tributes from across the climbing community he helped define.Whisenant, a Mammoth Lakes climber, built his reputation on some of the most demanding routes in American climbing. Yosemite's El Capitan, a granite wall rising thousands of feet above the valley floor, has long served as the sport's proving ground for big-wall specialists, and Whisenant became one of its most recognizable names.No cause of death has been confirmed. The coroner's office listed only the date, and no additional information had surfaced as of the initial reports.Bailee Moore, described as Whisenant's lifelong friend, confirmed his death in an Instagram post that circulated quickly among climbers. She wrote that her family was devastated but found some comfort knowing Whisenant died doing what he loved in the Sierra Nevada, and she closed her tribute with a personal message to him: "I will look for you in every life, my brother."The post drew an outpouring of condolences from fellow climbers and members of the broader climbing community, many of whom had followed Whisenant's rapid rise over the past two years. His death lands as a significant loss for a scene that had watched him push the limits of what speed climbing on El Capitan looked like.Whisenant gained national attention in October 2024 when he and South Lake Tahoe climber Brant Hysell completed the Lurking Fear route on El Capitan in 2 hours, 55 minutes and 32 seconds. Climbing magazine Gripped reported that the ascent broke the previous speed record held by Yuji Hirayama and Nick Fowler, a mark that had stood as one of the benchmarks in the sport.That record did not come without buildup. Whisenant and Hysell had already climbed the same route in just over four hours two days earlier, a pace that showed how quickly they were refining their approach before the record attempt.He kept pushing after that. In May, the Yosemite Climbing Association reported that Whisenant and fellow climber Noah Fox climbed The Nose, another of El Capitan's marquee routes, twice in a single day, finishing the double ascent in 14 hours and 38 minutes. The Nose is considered one of the classic big-wall climbs in Yosemite, and completing it twice in one push demands a level of sustained endurance few climbers attempt.Those achievements had turned Whisenant into a rising figure in Yosemite's increasingly competitive speed-climbing scene, one still absorbing the news that one of its fastest climbers is gone. Investigators have not said whether more information about the accident will be released.
Article Summary: Yosemite's El Capitan climber Jake Whisenant dies at 30 in a Sierra Nevada accident. The Tulare County Sheriff's Office Coroner recorded his date of death as August 3. Officials have not released details about the circumstances of the accident.

Article Title: “I want people to know this diagnosis doesn’t define me”: How NFL legend Roger Craig is confronting vascular dementia after doctors raised concerns about his concussion history
Article Text:
Roger Craig reveals dementia diagnosis (Getty Images)

What did Roger Craig reveal about his vascular dementia diagnosis?

How has Roger Craig responded to his diagnosis and NFL legacy?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Roger Craig used his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction to reveal a deeply personal health battle, announcing that he has been diagnosed with vascular dementia at 66. In a pre-taped speech shown Saturday, Aug. 8, the former San Francisco 49ers running back said doctors believe the condition “may be related, at least in part, to the concussions” he suffered during his 11-year NFL career. Craig said the changes in his health developed slowly and were first seen as part of normal aging. His decision to speak publicly added a personal dimension to an otherwise celebratory weekend.Roger Craig said his health changes “were gradual” and initially “dismissed as normal aging.” It was only after his family began noticing changes that he and those close to him sought medical advice.“Over time, my family noticed it too and ultimately led us to seek answers from my doctor,” the athlete continued. “Two things can be true: Football gave me opportunities beyond anything I could imagine. It helped shape the man I became. At the same time, we know more today about brain health than when I played, and I hope sharing my story encourages people to pay attention to their health and seek help when something doesn’t feel right.The Alzheimer’s Association describes vascular dementia as “a decline in thinking skills caused by conditions that block or reduce blood flow to various regions of the brain, depriving them of oxygen and nutrients.” Symptoms can include confusion, trouble finding words, problems with attention and planning, slowed thinking and memory difficulties, according to the Mayo Clinic.Craig did not attend the media conference held Thursday for the other members of the 2026 Hall of Fame class. Larry Fitzgerald, Drew Brees, Adam Vinatieri and Luke Kuechly each spoke with reporters during the event.His absence became more significant after the diagnosis was disclosed. Craig instead shared his story through the taped induction speech, choosing to address his health on his own terms.Craig has not separated his health battle from his feelings about football. He acknowledged the risks while making it clear that his career remains an important part of his identity.“Football gave me everything,” Craig reiterated. “I want people to know this diagnosis doesn’t define me.”“I am still Roger Craig. I am still a father, a husband, a teammate, a friend and someone who loves this game and the people who brought it to my life,” he added. “If sharing my story helps even one family or one former player, then it’s worth it.”That message carried extra weight during a weekend that marked the end of Craig’s long wait for Hall of Fame recognition. He spent 28 years waiting for enshrinement after a career that helped reshape what an NFL running back could do.Craig became the first NFL player to record 1,000 rushing yards and 1,000 receiving yards in the same season. Marshall Faulk and Christian McCaffrey are the only other players to match that feat, according to NBC Sports. Craig also made four Pro Bowls and won three Super Bowls with the 49ers during his 11 seasons with San Francisco, the Los Angeles Raiders and Minnesota Vikings.The 49ers made sure his presence was felt even as he remained away from the media spotlight. Coaches wore black shirts carrying “Craig” and “33” during practice Saturday, honoring one of the most influential players in franchise history.Craig's emotional weekend had already begun Friday, when former 49ers owner Eddie DeBartolo Jr. presented him with his gold jacket. Former teammate and childhood friend Jamie Williams later presented him for induction.The diagnosis did not erase those achievements. Instead, Craig used the biggest recognition of his football life to raise a broader point about health, awareness and asking for help when something feels different.
Article Summary: Former 49ers running back Roger Craig has been diagnosed with vascular dementia. Craig said doctors believe the condition “may be related, at least in part, to the concussions’ he suffered during his 11-year NFL career. Craig's decision to speak publicly added a personal dimension to an otherwise celebratory weekend. Craig used the biggest recognition of his football life to raise a broader point of awareness.

Article Title: "I've never considered myself famous": How Naomi Osaka kept her feet on the ground while becoming one of tennis’ biggest global stars
Article Text:
Naomi Osaka’s secret to staying grounded as fame (Getty Images)

Why does Naomi Osaka say she doesn't want to be famous?

How has Naomi Osaka's fashion changed her public image in 2026?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Naomi Osaka is a four-time Grand Slam champion, a former World No. 1, and one of the most talked-about athletes on the planet. And yet, the 28-year-old said something that stopped the room. She doesn't consider herself famous. Eight and a half years into a career that has reshaped women's tennis, Osaka's perspective on her own stardom remains almost stubbornly unchanged. For her, that is not a problem. It might actually be the point.Naomi Osaka's relationship with fame has always been a strange one. When she beat Daria Kasatkina 6-3, 6-2 at Indian Wells in March 2018 to claim her first WTA title, she thought that was it. The ceiling. Her mother, who had been working long hours, was finally able to retire because of that win, and for Osaka, nothing in tennis felt bigger than that moment."When I won Indian Wells, I for sure thought 'Wow, life can't get any crazier than this' because my mom was working all the time, and I rarely saw her, and she was able to retire because of that," Osaka said. "I felt like that was peak."Then came the 2018 US Open. Then the second US Open. Then two Australian Open titles.Then a mental health break that shifted the entire conversation around athlete wellbeing. Then a pregnancy, a daughter named Shai, and a comeback. Each chapter raised her profile further, and yet Osaka keeps arriving at the same conclusion."I actually don't really want to be famous, so I'm good with where I'm at right now," she said in Washington. "I feel like every moment has blips, and it's kind of just like always steadily going up. Whenever I think it's levelled out, something else keeps happening. I've never considered myself famous, so I've always done everything that I've done before now."There is something quietly radical about that. The world's press follows her every outfit change. Fashion houses track her Grand Slam walk-on looks. Sponsors line up. And through all of it, Osaka approaches Monday the same way she apparently approached the week before Indian Wells in 2018. Without the weight of the spotlight she never asked to carry.The fashion angle is new territory, and Osaka knows it. Throughout 2026, her on-court walk-on outfits at all three Grand Slams have drawn as much discussion as her tennis, sometimes more. For someone who describes herself as introverted, that is a deliberate decision, not a branding exercise."Ironically, wearing the outfits that I wear have kind of forced me to speak a lot more, especially about topics that I'm not necessarily an expert on," Osaka said. "Kind of branching out, doing the fashion stuff has made me talk to people that I've never met before and things like that. [I'm] just trying to go into worlds that I've never imagined myself sort of being in before."She even mentioned a preference for small, independent designers who are not household names. Which, in a way, sounds exactly like how she describes herself. Not someone chasing the biggest stage, but finding meaning in the spaces most people overlook.What's interesting is the bleed-over. Osaka said people now follow her more for fashion than for tennis. That could read as a threat to her athletic identity. She doesn't seem to see it that way. For her, it is just another blip in a career full of them, another moment she did not plan for but has learned to move through.Now she heads into the hard court swing, the surface where all four of her majors have come, with the US Open ahead. Osaka noted she can "only hope to be really optimistic" and play well. That word, hope, from someone with four Grand Slams, is worth sitting with. She is not coasting. She is still reaching.That, more than any outfit or quote about fame, tells you most of what you need to know about where Naomi Osaka is right now.
Article Summary: Naomi Osaka is a four-time Grand Slam champion, and a former World No. 1. The 28-year-old said she doesn't consider herself famous. Her on-court walk-on outfits at all three Grand Slams have drawn as much discussion as her tennis.

Article Title: Inspiring story of the day: “My dad made huge sacrifices. He worked extra hours.” - How Lionel Messi and his father turned illness, and family devotion into football immortality

What happened to Lionel Messi as a child

Why did Lionel Messi move to Barcelona at 13

How did Jorge Messi shape Lionel Messi’s career

Why does Lionel Messi’s family story still inspire fans

Lionel Messi’s rise to football greatness began with a problem that could have changed his entire future. As a child in Rosario, Argentina, Messi was diagnosed with a growth hormone deficiency and needed costly treatment. His family struggled to keep paying for it, while his father, Jorge Messi, worked to support him and find another solution. That search eventually took the 13-year-old Lionel to Barcelona in 2000, where the club agreed to cover his treatment. Years later, Messi became an eight-time Ballon d’Or winner and a World Cup champion, but his journey still begins with the family that stood behind him.Before Lionel Messi became one of football’s biggest names, his family was dealing with a serious problem. Messi was diagnosed with a growth hormone deficiency when he was young. The condition affected his growth and required regular hormone injections.The treatment was expensive. Reports have put the monthly cost at around $900 to $1,000, which was a major burden for a working-class family in Argentina. His father, Jorge Messi, worked at a steel company in Rosario, while his mother, Celia, worked as a magnet cleaner.The family received some help, including support connected to Messi’s football career, but paying for the treatment remained difficult. Local clubs could not provide a long-term answer, leaving Jorge with the difficult task of finding another way to keep his son’s treatment going.Jorge did not want Messi’s medical condition to decide what happened to his football career. He continued working and looking for a club that could help with the cost of treatment while also giving his son the chance to develop as a player.Messi has spoken about the sacrifices his father made during those years.“My dad made huge sacrifices for me to play football. He worked extra hours at the factory just so I could have my hormone treatments. Watching him work so hard for our family taught me what dedication really means.”For a young Messi, the treatment was necessary for his health, but football remained a major part of his life. His father’s support helped him continue both.The family eventually had to look outside Argentina for a long-term solution. Barcelona became that opportunity.In 2000, Lionel Messi travelled to Spain for a trial with FC Barcelona. He was only 13 years old. The move meant leaving behind Rosario, his friends and much of the family life he knew.Barcelona saw something special in the young Argentine. The club eventually agreed to take responsibility for his medical treatment and brought him into its youth system.That decision changed Messi’s life.The teenager now had to adjust to a new country while continuing his growth hormone treatment. He also had to settle into the demands of Barcelona’s youth academy, where expectations were high even for a player so young.Jorge stayed close to his son during this period. His presence gave Messi someone familiar to rely on while he dealt with the loneliness and pressure of being far from home.Messi later described how difficult the early period in Spain was:“It was very hard when I first arrived in Barcelona. I missed my family, my home, my friends. But my dad was always there with me. He was the one who kept me going when things were difficult and made sure I never felt alone.”The move was a huge risk for the family, but it gave Messi something he had not had before - a clear path to continue his treatment while pursuing football at the highest level.The young player who arrived in Barcelona eventually became the face of the club.Messi made his Barcelona first-team debut in 2004 and went on to become the club’s record goalscorer. During his time at Barcelona, he won four Champions League titles and numerous domestic trophies. He also became the first player to win eight Ballon d’Or awards.Jorge remained involved as his son’s representative and adviser as Messi’s career grew. The relationship that began with a father trying to help his young son through a difficult medical situation continued into the biggest stages of world football.Messi’s success with Argentina brought another important chapter.At the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar, Argentina reached the final against France. Messi scored twice during the match, and Argentina eventually won on penalties after a 3-3 draw.It was the World Cup title Messi had wanted throughout his international career.His family shared that moment with him. His wife, Antonela Roccuzzo, their children and other members of his family were part of the celebration as Messi finally lifted the biggest trophy in international football.The achievement also reflected how far he had come from the young boy who needed medical treatment just to keep developing physically.Messi has repeatedly spoken about the importance of his family in his career:“My family is everything to me. My father, my mother, my wife, my kids… every trophy I have won, every goal I have scored is for them. They suffered with me during the bad times and celebrated with me during the good times. Without my father’s sacrifices when I was a boy, none of this would have been possible.”For Messi, the World Cup was not only a personal achievement. It was also the result of years of work and support from the people closest to him.Messi is often remembered for his dribbling, goals, records and trophies. But his childhood explains another part of his story.He was not simply a talented boy who moved to Europe and became a star. His family first had to deal with a medical condition that required expensive treatment. They then had to make the difficult decision to send a 13-year-old to another country because it offered him a better chance.Jorge’s role went beyond paying bills or helping Messi reach Barcelona. He remained a steady presence as his son adjusted to life in Spain and later became one of the most important people in Messi’s professional career.The story also shows why Messi has remained so connected to his family despite spending much of his adult life in the spotlight.His career has brought eight Ballon d’Or awards, four Champions League titles with Barcelona and a World Cup with Argentina. Yet none of those achievements changes where the story began: with a young boy in Rosario, a difficult medical diagnosis and a family determined to help him continue playing football.The final quote supplied for this story reflects that connection:“Lionel Messi reached the absolute summit of world sport through unmatched natural genius and dedication, but his journey was made possible by the sacrifices of his father, Jorge. By honoring his roots and keeping his family at the heart of his career, he proves that the greatest victories in life are those shared with the ones who believed in you from the beginning.”Messi’s career will always be measured through goals, trophies and records. But behind those numbers is a much more personal story. His father worked to help pay for his treatment, stayed with him through a difficult move to Barcelona and remained involved as his career grew.That family support did not guarantee Messi success. His talent and hard work still had to carry him the rest of the way. But it gave a young boy the chance to find out just how far that talent could take him.
Article Summary: Lionel Messi was diagnosed with a growth hormone deficiency as a child. The condition affected his growth and required regular hormone injections. The treatment was expensive and the family struggled to pay for it. Messi's father, Jorge, worked extra hours to help pay for his son's treatment. Barcelona agreed to cover the cost of Messi's treatment when he was 13. Messi moved to Barcelona and became the club's record scorer.

Article Title: I'll continue playing, rest is selectors' call: Bhuvneshwar Kumar
Article Text:
Bhuvneshwar Kumar

After a hugely successful IPL where his pace paved the way for Royal Challengers Bengaluru’s fine title run through the season, Bhuvneshwar Kumar is currently sweating it out in the nets here for the upcoming UPT20 league, where he will spearhead Lucknow Falcons’ charge.En route to becoming the first pacer to take 200 wickets in the IPL, and finding praise for his effective Powerplay bowling with subtle variations alongside his swing this season, Bhuvneshwar showed he’s a chip off the old block with 28 scalps - 17 in the Powerplays - with an economy rate of 8.It immediately drew notice with even calls for him to be reinstated in India’s white ball set-up.Asked if he missed the India blue jersey or if he was eyeing for the 2027 World Cup, the seasoned right arm pacer told TOI, “I’m here to play, and that’s what I’m doing. My job is to play cricket; judging how prepared I am isn’t something that I focus on.“I haven’t come to play in the UPT20 League because I want to get picked somewhere or move to another level. I’m playing simply because I want to play,” the plain-speaking Bhuvneshwar said, “As for what the senior and veteran players are saying, that’s their opinion. For me, I enjoy playing and I love cricket. My job is only to play, and I’m here for the UPT20 League.“How prepared I am is not for me to decide; the rest is the selectors’ call,” he added.The 36-year-old, one of Uttar Pradesh’s most experienced cricketers, continues to remain a key figure in Indian domestic cricket. He last played for India in 2022, featuring in both ODI and T20I formats. His last international appearance in Tests came in 2018.A stalwart for the Uttar Pradesh Cricket Association, Bhuvneshwar has taken 231 wickets in 72 Ranji Trophy matches in the first-class circuit. He last played a Ranji Trophy match in 2024 against Mumbai.Asked on his possible participation in the upcoming Ranji season, Bhuvneshwar said there was still time before making a decision.“There’s still plenty of time, and a lot of cricket to be played before that. I can’t say right now whether I’ll play first-class cricket or not, but my aim is to keep playing as much cricket as I can,” the veteran pacer said.Last season, Uttar Pradesh struggled with a lack of depth in the pace department, following which the UPCA launched a speed hunt programme to identify and develop fast-bowling talent across the state.In hoping to continue with Uttar Pradesh’s tradition of producing fast bowlers such as Praveen Kumar , RP Singh, Sudip Tyagi and himself, Bhuvneshwar said the speed hunt initiative could help strengthen the team’s pace resources.“First-class cricket is a big season. Many fast bowlers got injured, and the lack of bowlers was visible. Through the speed hunt, we have found a bunch of pace bowlers from across the state. They were also seen in the UPT20 League, and one of the scouted players became the uncapped highest bidder in the mini-auction. Through this initiative, UPCA will nurture young pace talent. It will help in the domestic season,” Bhuvneshwar said.
Article Summary: Bhuvneshwar Kumar is the first pacer to take 200 wickets in the IPL. He last played for India in 2022, featuring in both ODI and T20I formats. His last international appearance in Tests came in 2018. The 36-year-old last played a Ranji Trophy match in 2024 against Mumbai.

Article Title: 19 days in jail, 'stole' police chair and deportation: Japanese student’s Bengaluru story
Article Text:
Hirotoshi Tanaka and the chair he 'stole' (Image Credit: Special arrangement)

A journey to Bengaluru

The 'stolen' chair (Image Credit: Special arrangement)

An unlikely friend in jail

An alleged bribery demand

A fight continues

The chair 'theft'

Seven years later





BENGALURU: When Japanese student Hirotoshi Tanaka came to Bengaluru in 2019, he had one simple plan — to learn English, experience life in India and eventually return to his parents in Yaizu city, Shizuoka, Japan.Instead, his journey took him from a police station to Bengaluru Central Prison, then to the Karnataka high court, the Karnataka State Human Rights Commission and eventually a detention centre before he was deported to Japan in April 2021.Nearly seven years after arriving in the city, Tanaka has now received Rs 75,000 in compensation from the Karnataka government after the human rights commission held that he had been unnecessarily kept in judicial custody for 19 days.But perhaps the most unusual chapter of his long legal battle came in the early hours of February 28, 2021, when Tanaka walked into the office of the JC Nagar assistant commissioner of police in RT Nagar, picked up a white plastic chair, took selfies with it and carried it back to his home in BTM Layout.He was not trying to steal the chair. He wanted the police to arrest him.Tanaka believed that an arrest would give him a way to remain in India while pursuing his human rights complaint.By then, he was struggling financially, his immigration status was uncertain and he had been ordered to leave the country.The chair, in his telling, was not about theft. It was a desperate attempt to force the police to notice him.But to understand how a Japanese student came to steal a police officer's chair just to get arrested, the story goes back to 2019.Tanaka, a 36-year-old psychology graduate at the time, arrived in Bengaluru and enrolled at a private English academyHe was dissatisfied with the academy after classes were allegedly cancelled frequently and conducted irregularly. He said repeated attempts to seek an explanation from the academy's head went unanswered, leading to growing tensions.The dispute eventually escalated into an argument. He alleged that he was then provoked, lost his temper and punched the academy head.Following the altercation, the RT Nagar police registered a case against him under charges of voluntarily causing hurt and criminal intimidation. Although the offences were bailable, Tanaka was arrested on November 23, 2019, and sent to Bengaluru Central Prison.He spent 19 days behind bars before being released on December 11.For a young Japanese student who had come to India to learn English, prison was a world away from what he had imagined.Looking back, Tanaka said the hardest part was not knowing what was happening to him or how he could get out.“I didn’t know anything about my case. Nothing was explained in the police station or before the magistrate,” he told TOI from Japan.“I didn’t know my section numbers. I didn’t even know legal terms like ‘advocate’, ‘bail’, ‘magistrate’, ‘custody’, ‘(criminal) case’ and so on. Initially I thought advocates meant friends or relatives so I was planning to ask cops of RT Nagar police station to be my advocate.”Not understanding the legal system or knowing how to secure his release made his time in prison particularly difficult.“That was a so surreal, kafkaesque experience. But thanks to criminals, jail police and jailers, I learned slowly about it in prison only. They were so supportive,” he said.Tanaka recalled that there was a section for foreign prisoners known as the “Negro Room”, where English-language films were shown.“I went to Negro Room just to watch films and get tomato curry they cooked. They were allowed to cook for themselves. Jail Sambar was tasted terrible. They purposely use less salt and spices for health of inmates. Vegetables used for curry was fresh though,” he said.He said he was intimidated by some of the inmates and therefore spent time in the psychiatric ward inside the prison hospital.Yet, amid the difficulties, Tanaka also encountered people who helped him.“The chief Superintendent allowed me to visit his office and gave me access to a computer,” he recalled.Then there was Shankar , who became his “closest friend”.“Shankar had been convicted of murdering three people but had become a deeply devoted Christian,” Tanaka said.“He accompanied me to the prison’s video-conference court hearings and stood by me when I had no money for bail. Without Shankar’s help, I don’t think I would have been able to leave prison.”Shankar was from Hubli and was shifted to Vijayapura jail in January 2020. Tanaka later gifted him items including a bag and keys.“I wish to meet him again. Shankar is very important person in my life,” Tanaka said.His health made his 19 days in prison even more difficult.Tanaka was taking medicines for ADHD (Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder) and insomnia before his arrest. But his medical certificate was not in English, and the prison doctor did not give him his medicines.“I was so sick for 19 days without my medicine. My medical certificate was in my suitcase in a hostel in Koramangala,” he said.Tanaka claimed the certificate, issued by his doctor in Japan, was written in English because he was travelling to India. However, he did not have it with him when he was arrested, as it was in his hostel. He said he was able to get his medication after he was released from prison.Tanaka said all his medicines were sedative ones, meaning the prison doctor could not prescribe them easily without the required medical documentation.Without his ADHD medication, he said, sounds became distorted, making it extremely difficult for him to understand spoken English.“My English wasn’t very good to begin with, so it made things even harder. Even the sound coming from the prison speakers seemed deafeningly loud to me,” he said.Tanaka's troubles did not end with his release.When he returned to the police station the following day to collect his belongings, he had very little money. He recalled that a constable, Raghavendra, noticed his financial condition and lent him Rs 1,500.However, Tanaka alleged that another officer, then sub-inspector, demanded a bribe from him.According to Tanaka, after negotiations he paid Rs 5,500, which also covered the amount he had borrowed. Days later, when he appeared before the court, he alleged that the officer again demanded Rs 3,000 to settle the case.Tanaka decided he would not simply pay and walk away.His father is a police officer in Japan, and Tanaka said he had great respect for the police. But he did not want to accept what he described as misconduct.“I wanted to fight,” he said.The legal battle, however, was not the only challenge he faced.With little money and nowhere to stay, Tanaka claimed he spent nights in RT Nagar Park before being robbed of his belongings. Fearing for his safety, he began sleeping inside the premises of the R. Nagar Police Station.One night, he lost consciousness and later woke up in the intensive care unit of Bowring Hospital.After being discharged in March 2020, a friend helped him find accommodation in BTM Layout.Then the Covid-19 pandemic brought another layer of uncertainty to his already complicated situation.Tanaka eventually approached the Karnataka high court, challenging the criminal proceedings against him.After the coaching centre's head agreed to settle the dispute, the HC, on November 2, 2020, quashed the FIR and all criminal proceedings against him.The criminal case that had resulted in his arrest and 19 days in prison was finally over.But Tanaka did not return to Japan.Instead, he decided to continue fighting what he believed was a larger injustice.In December 2020, Tanaka approached the Karnataka State Human Rights Commission, filing a complaint against an police offical, who has since retired.Tanaka told TOI that the idea to approach the commission came from an unexpected encounter at a hostel. He said the brother of a DCP advised him to take his case to the Human Rights Commission after the two met by chance and discussed his situation.According to Tanaka, the suggestion eventually led him to file his complaint against then RT Nagar police sub-inspector, who has since retired.Tanaka alleged that the officer had demanded a bribe from him to drop the case. He wanted action against the officer and also wanted the police department to bear his travel expenses.But while he pursued the human rights complaint, his immigration status was becoming increasingly difficult.His visa had expired while the criminal case was still pending. In March 2020, before the Covid-19 lockdown, officials from the Consulate-General of Japan in Bengaluru approached the police on his behalf, but were told that the matter was before the court, Tanaka said.After the criminal case was quashed, the Foreigners Regional Registration Office directed Tanaka to leave India before February 28, 2021.Tanaka did not want to leave.He wanted to stay in India until his complaint before the human rights commission was addressed. At the same time, he said he was struggling financially and needed medicines.Tanaka told TOI that his immigration problems continued even after the criminal case was quashed.“My new visa was granted in July 2020 which was valid till Sep 2020. And it was extended till March 2021 as my criminal case was still pending. My case was quashed by the Karnataka high court November 2, 2020 so exit permit was issued and it worked as my visa. It was valid till the end of Dec 2020 but I didn’t return to Japan as I filed a complaint against the police before the Karnataka State Human Rights Commission.”Tanaka said that after he stayed back in India to pursue the complaint, the Foreigners Regional Registration Office filed a complaint against him at Mico Layout police station near his hostel in BTM Layout.“After some negotiations, Exit permit was extended till Feb 2021. The first hearing was scheduled in Febuary but the police didn’t not send the report on my case so it was postponed. I applied for extension of my exit permit but it had been under process for a couple of weeks.”Tanaka said he wanted to remain in India to attend the hearing but was also struggling financially.As the February 28 deadline approached, Tanaka came up with an unusual plan.He believed that if he committed a minor offence and was arrested, he could remain in India while pursuing his complaint.“I wish to attend the hearing and I though I I had to but I was penniless and application for new exit permit had been pending. So to clear my financing problems and visa problem I committed “theft”. But nothing happened," he said.And that was when the plastic chair entered the story.Around 1am on February 28, Tanaka entered the JC Nagar ACP's office at RT Nagar. He picked up a white plastic chair from the reception area.Then he photographed himself with it. He carried the chair back to his home in BTM Layout and waited.There was no attempt to hide what he had done. Tanaka wanted the police to know.More importantly, he wanted them to arrest him. His reasoning was simple: an arrest, he believed, would allow him to remain in India while continuing his legal battle.It was an extraordinary move, but by then Tanaka's options appeared limited. He had already spent 19 days in prison, had fought to get the criminal case quashed and was now facing an order to leave the country while his human rights complaint remained unresolved.The chair was never really about the chair.It was his desperate attempt to force the authorities to notice him.The human rights commission rules in his favourAfter eventually returning to Japan, Tanaka continued pursuing the case through his Bengaluru-based advocate Rohan Kothari.Following an inquiry, the Karnataka State Human Rights Commission ruled in his favour on May 9, 2022.The commission concluded that police officials had failed to justify his arrest in a case involving bailable offences, resulting in his unnecessary judicial custody for 19 days.The commission recommended that the Karnataka government pay Tanaka Rs 75,000 as compensation.It also recommended disciplinary proceedings against the police offical, recovery of the compensation amount from the officer and guidelines for police dealing with foreign nationals and illiterate persons during arrests.But the recommendations were not immediately implemented.Tanaka alleged that after waiting for months, he was still not paid the compensation.In September 2022, he approached the Karnataka High Court seeking enforcement of the commission's order.The legal battle continued for years.This year, the State government informed the high court that it would comply with the KSHRC's recommendations. In April, the State filed an affidavit stating that Rs 75,000 would be transferred to Tanaka through his counsel and that disciplinary proceedings had been initiated against Hanumantharayappa.The compensation was finally paid to Kothari on June 22.Tanaka's advocate then transferred the amount to his Indian wife's account on June 23.“My bank in Japan didn’t handle Indian Rupee so I asked Rohan to get the compensation. I think I can say I got 75k from Karnataka,” Tanaka said.For Tanaka, the Rs 75,000 is the culmination of a legal battle that began with a dispute at an English academy and took him through a prison cell, courtrooms, an immigration fight and a human rights complaint.But his memories of Bengaluru are not entirely defined by the ordeal.He remembers the prison officials who helped him navigate a legal system he knew nothing about. He remembers the “Negro Room”, the tomato curry and the computer he was allowed to use in the chief superintendent's office.And he remembers Shankar, the prisoner convicted of murdering three people who became his closest friend during the darkest period of his stay in India.Tanaka still wishes to meet him again.Speaking to TOI, Tanaka said he now wants to return to India, particularly to visit his wife's hometown in the Northeast and meet her family.Asked whether he hopes to return to India someday, Tanaka said. “Yes. My wife is from North East and I wish to visit her hometown and meet her relatives as soon as possible. But I am still blacklisted thanks to deportation in 2021 so cannot reenter India. Now an advocate bases in Mumbai(not Rohan Kothari in Bangalore) is trying to have my name removed from blacklist.”For the Japanese student who came to Bengaluru to learn English, the city ultimately gave him an experience he could never have anticipated — 19 days in prison, an alleged encounter with police bribery, a prolonged legal battle, an unusual attempt to get arrested with a plastic chair and, nearly seven years later, Rs 75,000 in compensation from the Karnataka government.The chair was never about stealing a chair. For Tanaka, it was a desperate plea to be heard.
Article Summary: Hirotoshi Tanaka came to Bengaluru in 2019 to learn English and experience life in India. He has now received Rs 75,000 in compensation from the Karnataka government. The human rights commission held that he had been unnecessarily kept in judicial custody for 19 days.

Article Title: ‘I don’t care how old he is’: Brett Lee’s big warning for Vaibhav Sooryavanshi
Article Text:
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi (AP Photo)

‘This kid can play cricket’

‘It’ll only be his mind’

How Lee would have bowled to Sooryavanshi

NEW DELHI: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has already made a remarkable impression on the cricketing world at 15, and Australia pace great Brett Lee believes the teenager has everything required to achieve “bigger and better things” — provided he is protected from the pressure accompanying his rapid rise.Sooryavanshi became one of the biggest stories of IPL 2026 after an extraordinary campaign for Rajasthan Royals . The left-hander scored 776 runs in 16 matches to claim the Orange Cap, repeatedly displaying a fearless approach against some of the world's best bowlers.His performances earned him a fast-track call-up to India's T20I side. After a difficult start to international cricket during the England series, Sooryavanshi responded impressively on India's Zimbabwe tour, finishing as Player of the Series.For Lee, however, the teenager's age should not overshadow what he is already doing on the field.Sooryavanshi's age has become a constant talking point outside India, but Lee believes the focus should be on his ability rather than the number attached to his name.“He is incredible. Everyone offshore, away from India, asks the question if he's 15. He is 15 is probably the biggest talking point around the world. I don't care how old he is.If he's 15, fantastic, but if he's 17 or 18, who cares. This kid can play cricket. He has been such a great find for India, and he's going to go on to achieve bigger and better things,” Lee said on the BeerBiceps YouTube channel.The former Australia fast bowler was particularly impressed by Sooryavanshi's ability to take on express pace during the IPL, including against Australian quicks.“He has already lit up the IPL in such a short space of time. That 97 he got (vs SRH), he was up against Aussie bowlers. They were bowling gas, and he was hooking them off his nose. He is playing proper cricketing shots and has power that he finds from somewhere,” Lee said.While Lee sees little reason to worry about Sooryavanshi's batting or current form, he believes the mental side of the game will be the biggest test as expectations continue to grow.“It won't be his form or batting; it'll only be his mind. He still has to be a kid. Let him be a kid and don't put too much pressure,” Lee said.The warning comes after Sooryavanshi's rapid transition from teenage prospect to IPL star and then an India international. The attention surrounding him is only likely to increase as he continues to perform at the highest level.Lee also offered an insight into how he would have approached the challenge of bowling to the teenager, particularly given Sooryavanshi's confidence against short-pitched deliveries.“If someone was a good hooker or puller of the ball, I used to love that because then it becomes a contest. So of course I would go into the boardroom, go upstairs and have a look. I'll put one on his badge and see what he does with it. He might hook me for six, but it won't discourage me from giving him another one,” Lee said.For a player who has already shown he is not intimidated by reputation or pace, such contests could become a defining feature of Sooryavanshi's early career.But Lee's message is clear: the teenager's biggest battle may not be against fast bowlers at all. It may be learning to handle everything that comes with being cricket's latest teenage sensation.
Article Summary: Brett Lee believes Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has everything required to achieve “bigger and better things’ The former Australia fast bowler believes the teenager's mental side of the game will be the biggest test as expectations continue to grow. Lee also offered an insight into how he would have approached the teenager.

Article Title: ‘CoE is not merely a rehab centre’: VVS Laxman speaks out as India’s injury crisis puts BCCI facility under scanner
Article Text:
VVS Laxman

‘We don't use the term blame’

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe injuries are an unavoidable part of a cricketer career? Yes, they are part of the sport. No, better management can prevent them. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia meets VVS Laxman

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: With India's growing injury list putting the spotlight on the BCCI Centre of Excellence (CoE), its head VVS Laxman has pushed back against the scrutiny surrounding the Bengaluru-based facility, insisting that injuries are an unavoidable part of a cricketer's career and that the focus should be on monitoring players rather than finding scapegoats.The CoE has come under increasing scrutiny in recent weeks amid concerns over rehabilitation timelines, fitness assessments and communication between its sports science team and the national selection committee. Several key players are currently dealing with injuries, with Jasprit Bumrah, Sai Sudharsan, Harshit Rana, Nitish Kumar Reddy and Washington Sundar among those facing fitness concerns.Laxman, however, defended the institution's broader role, stressing that it should not be reduced to a rehabilitation centre."CoE is not merely a rehab centre. There are bigger roles to play for it in helping cricketers achieve excellence," Laxman said at a press conference in Bengaluru on Sunday.His comments come at a time when the CoE's injury-management programme is under renewed examination, particularly with India set to begin a crucial Test series against Sri Lanka on August 15.Laxman also refused to attribute India's injury problems to any individual or department, arguing that injuries are an inherent part of professional sport."Injuries are part and parcel of any player's career. That's why monitoring system is very critical. And we don't use the term blame then we will be trying to find scapegoats," he said.The CoE chief pointed towards the facility's monitoring systems and the measures being used to assess players continuously, rather than relying solely on conventional fitness tests."Yo Yo test cannot be done when a player is part of the series, so we have introduced Bronco test by Adrian, so that the fitness can be monitored continously," Laxman said.He cited Bumrah and Sudharsan as examples of players whose fitness was assessed through multiple parameters before decisions were made on their availability."Jasprit Bumrah and B Sai Sudharsan were picked as subject to fitness. We move them from one parameter to other before giving the clearance to play. The communication between CoE and team management is quite seamless," he added.The comments are significant given the uncertainty that has surrounded the availability of both Bumrah and Sudharsan for the Sri Lanka Tests.Both players were initially included in India's squad subject to fitness, but the CoE's medical and sports science experts ultimately opted for caution after assessing their respective conditions.Bumrah's absence is particularly significant, with the fast bowler's knee continuing to cause problems after an impact injury. Don Nelson, the second-winningest coach in NBA history, died Sunday at age 86, his family announced. Luka Doncic learned of the news while speaking to reporters and immediately offered condolences to the family of the Hall of Fame coach who once wore Doncic's sneakers in protest of his trade out of Dallas.The tribute carried extra weight given Doncic's ties to the Nelson family. He recently partnered with Nelson's son, longtime Mavericks executive Donnie Nelson, to buy Italian club Vanoli Cremona. A cause of death has not been disclosed.Doncic's connection to Nelson went beyond typical player-to-legend admiration. Nelson became one of Doncic's most vocal defenders after Dallas stunned the league by trading him to the Los Angeles Lakers in 2025. During the 2025 NBA Finals, Nelson accepted the Chuck Daly Lifetime Achievement Award while wearing Doncic's signature shoes, calling the trade a "tremendous mistake."Doncic reflected on that support in his own tribute. It’s a sad day for basketball with the passing of Don Nelson. “I have so much respect for him and everything he did for the game, especially the way he believed in international players. I’m grateful for the time I spent with him,” he said, adding that he was grateful for the time they spent together and had deep respect for how Nelson championed international players.“Thinking of the entire Nelson family today. I loved getting to know you, Coach.”The Mavericks organization echoed that sentiment. Governor Patrick Dumont said Nelson brought "a winning culture to Dallas" that still shapes the franchise today. NBA commissioner Adam Silver credited Nelson with revolutionizing the sport, noting his "fearlessness, ingenuity and deep conviction" across nearly five decades in the league.Dirk Nowitzki, who Nelson coached during his rise to superstardom in Dallas, delivered one of the day's most personal tributes. "You didn't just draft me. You believed in me," Nowitzki wrote, crediting Nelson with giving him the freedom to develop into a Hall of Famer.Nelson's bond with the Doncic era traces back further than his coaching tenure. Donnie Nelson helped engineer the 2018 draft-night trade that sent Trae Young and a future first-round pick to Atlanta for the rights to Doncic, a move that reshaped the Mavericks for a decade.Golden State's ties to Nelson run just as deep. He coached the Warriors across two stints, including the "We Believe" run in 2007 that produced the biggest upset in NBA playoff history when the eighth-seeded Warriors knocked off Doncic's old team, the 67-win Mavericks.Stephen Curry, who Golden State drafted in 2009 during Nelson's second stint as coach, credited Nelson directly for his opportunity. "He had an immeasurable impact on the sport," Curry said, recalling that Nelson challenged him from his first day despite a reputation for being skeptical of rookies.Warriors coach Steve Kerr, who also played briefly under Nelson, praised his lasting influence on the modern game. "So much of what is now commonplace in the modern NBA can be traced back to the way Nellie approached the game," Kerr said.The Warriors organization released its own statement calling Nelson "an iconic figure in Warriors history" whose innovative approach shaped both the Run TMC era and the 2007 upset squad.The team pointed to his 1,335 career wins and his role in popularizing small-ball lineups that influence today's league.Nelson's family has not disclosed a cause of death. He is survived by his wife, Joy, and his family, including Donnie Nelson.Nelson's coaching résumé remains one of the most decorated in league history. He won three Coach of the Year awards, seven consecutive division titles with Milwaukee from 1980-86, and built the Warriors and Mavericks into playoff contenders during his respective tenures. His No. 2 ranking on the all-time wins list sits behind only Gregg Popovich.For now, the tributes from Doncic and Curry stand as the clearest sign of how far Nelson's influence reached, from the players he drafted to the ones he simply refused to give up on decades later.

Why the Clavicular steroid controversy is drawing attention

Clavicular has built a major online identity around looksmaxxing and physical appearance, but a fresh controversy is putting his claims under a harsh spotlight. A post circulating on X attributes a blunt critique to fitness personality Greg Doucette, who questioned whether Clavicular’s public image matches his alleged approach to performance and physique. The comments have quickly turned attention toward the growing debate over steroids, testosterone use and authenticity in online fitness culture.The controversy centers on remarks attributed to Greg Doucette in the post shared by Clavicular Updates. Doucette reportedly challenged the idea of Clavicular presenting himself as a natural figure within the looksmaxxing space.The post quotes him saying:“Clavicular, the face of looksmaxxing, isn’t looksmaxxing! It’s like a financial advisor not having any money, not saving, wasting it all, or a marriage counselor who’s been through 5 divorces, How is that possible?”The criticism then became more pointed, with Doucette allegedly questioning claims about Clavicular’s reported use of performance-enhancing substances.“Apparently Clavicular is natural, because realistically he is, besides the fact he’s been abusing steroids since the age of 14, despite the fact he’s on 10 mg of Reta(trutide) right now... Does this look like a guy who is on high doses of HRT? A guy who has essentially lost all of his muscle... If Clavicular is on 200 mg of test a week and/or more, that is not TRT, that is a low dose (ster-id) cycle.”These are serious claims, and they should be treated as allegations rather than established facts.The image does not provide independent evidence proving that Clavicular used steroids from a particular age or that he is currently taking any specific substance or dosage.The dispute goes beyond one influencer or one viral post. Clavicular has become closely associated with the looksmaxxing movement, a broad online culture focused on improving physical appearance through grooming, fitness, style and other methods.That makes claims about his own physique especially sensitive. If an influencer promotes a particular approach to appearance while allegedly relying on methods that are not openly disclosed, audiences may question how much of the transformation is attainable naturally.Doucette’s comparison is built around that perceived contradiction. His central argument is not simply about appearance. It is about credibility.The controversy also highlights a bigger problem in online fitness spaces. Viewers often see dramatic physiques, rapid transformations and confident claims without knowing the full story behind them. Some creators openly discuss performance-enhancing drugs, while others deny using them. In many cases, audiences are left trying to separate documented information from speculation.For Clavicular, the latest criticism adds another layer to an already highly scrutinized online persona. The accusations circulating in the post may generate plenty of discussion, but they do not independently establish steroid use or prove the specific medical claims being made.That distinction matters. Viral fitness controversies can spread far faster than evidence.For now, the biggest takeaway is the challenge Doucette’s alleged comments have placed before Clavicular: whether the image presented online accurately reflects the methods behind his physique. Until verifiable evidence emerges, the steroid-related allegations remain claims rather than confirmed facts.

The basketball world is mourning today at the loss of NBA legend and Hall of Famer Don Nelson, who breathed his last on Sunday at the age of 86. The news of his death was confirmed in a statement shared by his family and NBA insider Mark Stein on Sunday.According to the family, Nelson peacefully passed away surrounded by his loved ones, and family members who were with him in his last moments. However, the cause of death has not been disclosed yet.It is important to note that Nelson has been a five-time NBA champion as a player with the Boston Celtics and later became a three-time NBA Coach of the Year and finished his coaching career with 1,335 regular-season victories. Basketball legend and three-time NBA Coach of the Year Don Nelson leaves behind an influential basketball legacy as he breathed his last on Sunday afternoon in Frisco, Texas. He was 86 at the time of his death. During his final moments, he was surrounded by his friends, family members, and loved ones.Sharing the news of his death, the family members said in a statement, "On Sunday morning, our beloved husband, dad, grandfather, and great-grandfather Don Nelson peacefully went to be with the Lord, surrounded by his loving family.Throughout his last week, friends and family encircled him with love, sharing the blessing of his friendship and revisiting treasured memories.”Don Nelson is known for being the second winning coach in NBA history, a five-time NBA champion as a player, and a member of the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame. He was inducted as a Hall of Famer in the year 2012 for his contribution to the league.Nelson was a legendary figure who won five championships as a player with the Boston Celtics from 1963 to 1976, leading the league in field goal percentage in 1975. During that period, Nelson played a central role in transforming the Mavericks into a legitimate Western Conference contender.Not only with the Mavericks, but his coaching career also included successful stints with the Milwaukee Bucks, Golden State Warriors, and New York Knicks. He ultimately finished his career with 1,335 wins.However, his final coaching stint came with Golden State, where he helped guide the Warriors during the early stages of Stephen Curry’s NBA career. Nelson retired from coaching in 2010 after a career spanning more than three decades on the sidelines.Apart from this, in 2025, Nelson was granted the Chuck Daly Lifetime Achievement Award. He wore Luka Doncic's shoes to "protest" the trade out of Dallas, which he called a "tremendous mistake,” as per Sports Illustrated.Although Nelson never won an NBA championship as a head coach, his influence went beyond the title count. His death leaves behind an enduring legacy that will be remembered for generations in the history of basketball.

Article Title: Who was Sydney Towle? TikTok star who inspired millions while documenting her cancer journey dies at 26
