TikTok creator Sydney Towle has died at 26 after a nearly three-year battle with cholangiocarcinoma, a rare bile duct cancer. Known for documenting her cancer journey with honesty and optimism, she inspired millions by promoting awareness and self-advocacy. Her family confirmed her passing, while fans and celebrities, including Alyssa Milano, paid heartfelt tributes. Towle's resilience, positivity and determination left a lasting impact on countless people around the world.

Who was Sydney Towle before TikTok knew her story?

The diagnosis that changed everything

Why Sydney Towle chose to share her cancer journey

The online criticism she faced

How her followers responded after her death

Why Sydney Towle's story resonated with young people

Sydney Towle spent nearly three years showing the internet what courage looked like. Even as an aggressive cancer reshaped her life, the 26-year-old creator refused to let it define her spirit. Her death has left millions grieving, but the messages pouring across social media make one thing clear. Her honesty, optimism and determination created a legacy that will outlive every viral video she ever posted.Before becoming a familiar face on TikTok, Sydney Towle was a young woman with big ambitions and an infectious personality. Living in New York City, she loved fashion, spending time with friends and documenting everyday moments that felt authentic rather than curated. Her content reflected joy long before cancer entered the picture.As her online audience grew to more than one million followers on TikTok and over 200,000 on Instagram, people connected with her openness and warm personality. Even after receiving a life-changing diagnosis, she continued to celebrate milestones.One of her proudest moments came when she fulfilled a longtime dream by walking the runway during The Chemo Club x Post Swim show at Miami Swim Week.It became a powerful reminder that illness did not erase her dreams.Towle was diagnosed with cholangiocarcinoma, a rare and aggressive bile duct cancer. Over time, the disease spread to other areas of her body, including her peritoneum, the membrane surrounding the abdominal and pelvic organs.She underwent years of chemotherapy and numerous treatments while documenting both the victories and setbacks. In May, she revealed that her oncologist had stopped treating her cancer and recommended end-of-life care. Rather than giving up, she sought another specialist and remained determined to keep fighting.Her family announced her passing in a heartfelt message."Syd went peacefully last night after an almost three-year-long battle with cholangiocarcinoma."They also honored the purpose she found through her platform."We are so proud of how hard Sydney fought and for sharing her journey with so many people. She wanted to raise awareness for rare cancers and was passionate about promoting self-advocacy. We will continue her legacy and honour her in every way we can."Towle never hid the difficult realities of cancer. She showed hospital stays, treatment days, emotional lows and joyful moments with equal honesty.She even embraced the scars left by treatment, including the hepatic artery pump implanted in her body. Instead of hiding it, she used it to encourage others struggling with body image and illness.Her social media often balanced painful updates with hope."Rich in life because my friends choose to spend a Saturday fundraising for cancer research."She also reminded followers to appreciate life's simple pleasures."Go get a pint of Ben and Jerry's, watch your favourite movie, remember that life is good and bad things happen sometimes but that doesn't make it a bad life."In another deeply personal reflection, she wrote:"I have only recently started seeing the resilience and beauty in this body. Scars that remind me of how far I've come. And I'm reminded that dreams only end when you allow them to."Being transparent online also exposed Towle to criticism. Some questioned her appearance, while others misunderstood why she continued posting during treatment.She rarely allowed negativity to shape her message. Instead, she focused on educating people about rare cancers, encouraging early medical attention and reminding others that every patient's experience is different. Her content remained centered on hope rather than conflict, earning admiration for its honesty and resilience.The announcement of Towle's death prompted an overwhelming response across social media. Thousands shared tributes celebrating the impact she had on their lives.Actress Alyssa Milano wrote:"Sweet angel. Fly high. Praying for all who loved her. She is really something special."Other followers echoed the same feelings."You were such a bright light and will be missed."Another tribute read:"How lucky we all are to have found you on the internet. Thank you for sharing yourself and your story."The messages reflected how deeply strangers had connected with someone they had never met in person.Sydney Towle's influence stretched beyond social media numbers. She gave young adults facing illness someone who understood their fears without pretending everything was perfect. She spoke honestly about pain while still making room for laughter, friendship and hope.Her videos became more than updates. They became reminders that resilience can exist alongside vulnerability. By sharing every chapter of her journey, Towle transformed personal hardship into a source of comfort for countless people, ensuring her voice will continue inspiring others long after her final post.
Article Summary: Sydney Towle was diagnosed with cholangiocarcinoma, a rare and aggressive bile duct cancer. Her death has left millions grieving, but the messages pouring across social media make one thing clear. Her honesty, optimism and determination created a legacy that will outlive every viral video.

At an age when most people slow down, 97-year-old Betty Bromage has once again taken to the skies, this time to break her own Guinness World Record as the oldest female wing walker.The Cheltenham resident completed the daring challenge by being strapped to the top of an aircraft as it flew through the sky, raising money for the stroke unit at Cheltenham General Hospital, where she received treatment after suffering a stroke in 2025.The feat marks Bromage's sixth wing walk, with her first completed at the age of 87. She had previously set the Guinness World Record four years ago and has now reclaimed the title by surpassing her own achievement.Bromage suffered a stroke in 2025, which continues to affect her speech, but she said she was determined not to let it stop her from doing what she loves."They treated me so well," she told BCC, referring to the hospital staff who cared for her. "It affects my words, but the rest of me is fine."Her latest wing walk was organised to raise funds for the hospital's stroke unit as a way of thanking the medical team that helped her during her recovery.According to the hospital's charity, donations from the fundraiser will help purchase equipment that will benefit both patients and healthcare staff.Despite approaching her 100th birthday, Bromage says she has no plans to give up adventurous challenges."I'd just get bored of life otherwise," she said. "I can't drive, I can't see very well and I get a bit frustrated. So, I want to do the things I can do."Known for her fearless spirit, Bromage joked that the most difficult part of wing walking isn't flying through the air, it's climbing onto the aircraft."The only problem is getting up on the wing because I'm quite short. Once you're up there, no problem. The fairground is a lot worse," she said with a laugh.A former nurse, Bromage said her passion for fundraising was inspired by a quote she once saw displayed on a hospital wall."We pass through this world but once. Any good we can do, any kindness we can show, do it now. Do not defer or neglect it. You will not pass this way again," she recalled.She said those words have stayed with her throughout her life and continue to motivate her charitable work.Hospital charity representative Imogen Sims praised Bromage's extraordinary determination, saying staff were grateful for her support."To take on such a daring challenge to support our team is amazing," Sims said, adding that the funds raised would make a real difference for patients and staff alike.As for what's next, Bromage is already thinking ahead."I'll have to think of something when I'm 100," she said. "Something special."Her latest record-breaking wing walk has once again proven that age is no barrier to adventure, or to giving back to the community.
Article Summary: Betty Bromage, 97, breaks her own Guinness World Record as oldest female wing walker. Cheltenham resident completed the challenge by being strapped to the top of an aircraft as it flew through the sky. Bromage suffered a stroke in 2025, which continues to affect her speech, but she said she was determined not to let it stop her from doing what she loves.

Article Title: How AIIMS Delhi turned a 70-yr-old donor's kidneys into new hope
Article Text:
AIIMS Delhi successfully performed a dual kidney transplant using organs from an elderly donor

Key pointers





NEW DELHI: A 70-year-old deceased woman's kidneys, which might otherwise have gone unused because of her age, have helped save a 56-year-old woman at AIIMS Delhi.Doctors say the hospital's second successful dual kidney transplant from an elderly 'marginal donor' highlights the potential of using carefully selected older donor organs to help address India's shortage of kidneys for transplantation.The transplant was performed on July 28 using the kidneys that came on an Army helicopter from Command Hospital in Chandigarh's Chandimandir.Because of the donor's advanced age, surgeons transplanted both kidneys into a single recipient, a strategy that helps provide adequate kidney function while maximising the use of organs that might otherwise be declined.The kidneys, which remained preserved outside the body for nearly 12 hours, started functioning immediately after surgery. The recipient recovered without complications and was discharged after 10 days with normal kidney function.Doctors said the case demonstrated the value of marginal donors, a category that included people above 60 years or those with conditions such as hypertension or diabetes.In selected cases, transplanting both kidneys into one recipient allows organs from such donors to be successfully utilised.The transplant surgery was led by prof Asuri Krishna of the surgical disciplines department, with support from nephrologists prof D Bhowmik and prof Sandeep Mahajan, while the anaesthesia team was headed by prof Vimi Rewari.The organ retrieval, transport and transplantation were coordinated by Organ Retrieval Banking Organisation, AIIMS Dual kidney transplantation is an important strategy for expanding access to transplantation for patients with end-stage kidney disease, stated AIIMS.According to the institute, this was its second such successful transplant, demonstrating that carefully selected kidneys from elderly donors can provide excellent early outcomes while increasing the use of organs.
Article Summary: AIIMS Delhi successfully performed a dual kidney transplant using organs from an elderly donor. The transplant was performed on July 28 using the kidneys that came on an Army helicopter from Command Hospital in Chandigarh's Chandimandir. The recipient recovered without complications and was discharged after 10 days with normal kidney function.
